name: Anushka Mittal

fix_next: Reconcile the cover's 3.8x with slide 7's 3.75x and document how the 784-row denominator was derived.
verdict: Exceptional thesis and method with minor internal inconsistencies.
factual_error_detail: Slide 1 states 3.8x recurring revenue multiple; slide 7 shows 3.75x median. This is a minor rounding inconsistency but still a mismatch within the deck. No other verifiable factual errors found.

evidence.insight: Constructs a novel recurring-share metric (MRR÷revenue), segments the dataset into three tiers, tests valuation premium with Mann-Whitney U (p=0.007), controls for size via partial correlation (0.26), and builds a tercile analysis showing the discount deepens with scale (slide 8). The arbitrage thesis on slide 10-11 is decision-useful and specific to three audiences.
evidence.narrative: Textbook hypothesis-driven arc: question (slide 3) → three sequential tests (exists? changes asset? market pays?) → supporting evidence that recurrence is engineerable (slide 9) → audience-segmented implications (slide 10) → actionable recommendation (slide 11) → memorable close (slide 12). Every slide advances the argument without redundancy.
evidence.framing: Slide 3 states hypothesis clearly. Slide 4 defines the metric, explains the 30-day window, shows the funnel (1000→784→380→215), and acknowledges churn is not reported. Slide 11 includes a falsifiability caveat. Audience made explicit on slide 10 (investors, founders, acquirers). Missing: no mention of survivorship bias or platform selection effects.
evidence.accuracy: 784 = 1000−216 zero-revenue rows matches frozen data. 151/784 = 19.3% ≈ 19% checks out. $13,499/$1,682 = 8.03x supports '8x' claim. 3.75/1.90−1 = 97.4% supports '+97%'. Cover says 3.8x but slide 7 says 3.75x — minor internal inconsistency. The 1.9x one-time median cannot be cross-checked against frozen reference (which gives B2B/B2C medians of 2.35x/2.30x, not one-time/recurring split). Mann-Whitney with n=29 is acknowledged as small but not flagged as a limitation.
evidence.visual: Consistent dark navy/white/gold palette across all 12 slides. Clear hierarchy with section labels. Bar charts with direct labels, no gridline clutter. Effective callout boxes for key stats. Case-study comparison table on slide 6 is well-designed. Grouped bar on slide 8 is appropriate. No chartjunk or decorative elements. Density is well-managed throughout.
evidence.ai_slop: none

change_reason: no-change. Preliminary scores are well-calibrated. The cover 3.8x vs 3.75x mismatch is minor (rounding), warranting 1 factual error rather than 2. All other scores hold upon close re-examination.

name: Anushka Tyagi

fix_next: Fix the $13.5M total (actual $15.6M) and reconcile the pie chart's 73% US share with the text's 63%.

factual_error_detail: Slide 2: Total MRR stated as $13.5M; actual 30-day revenue is $15.6M (and MRR ≠ revenue). Slide 4: Pie chart shows US at 73.05% but text says 63%—internally contradictory; $9.84M/15.6M ≈ 63%, so the pie is wrong. Slide 4: Title says '26% of Startups' but 258/1000=25.8% among all, and 258 is 25.8% not 26% (minor). Slide 9: Provider shares shown as percentages of only 5 providers (sum ~100%) but presented as if they are the full market; Paddle (16 companies) and Superwall (17) are omitted, making the pie misleading. Slide 8: Claims B2B achieves 'consistently higher revenue-per-customer' without showing any supporting data from the dataset; the actual median multiples (B2B 2.35× vs B2C 2.30×) are nearly identical.

evidence.insight: Slide 3's mean/median gap observation is genuinely useful; slide 7's revenue-per-visitor calculation adds value. But slides 10-14 repeat the same thesis without new data, and 'valuation multiples' discussion on slide 10 references no actual multiples from the dataset.
evidence.narrative: There is a clear through-line: power law → geography → category → monetization → thesis. The arc is coherent but the last four slides (11-14) are repetitive summaries that add no new evidence, padding the deck.
evidence.framing: No mention of missingness (241 country, 274 category, 288 audience_type missing). Audience is implicitly VC investors but never stated. No limitations slide. 'Revenue-generating companies across all verticals' on slide 2 is misleading—216 have zero revenue.
evidence.accuracy: Slide 2 headline figure $13.5M is wrong (total 30-day revenue is $15.6M). Slide 4 pie chart (73.05% US) contradicts its own text (63%). Provider pie omits Paddle and Superwall. evidence.visual: Gamma template throughout with decorative AI-generated illustrations on 6 of 14 slides that add no information. Only 2 actual data charts (slides 3 and 6). Slide 8's abstract bubble diagram is decorative, not data-driven. Pie charts on slides 4 and 9 are functional but one is factually wrong. Heavy text density on slides 11-12.

Decorative stock illustrations on slides 1, 5, 7, 10, 13 add nothing. Slides 11-14 are nearly interchangeable strategy summaries with no new data. Risk/mitigation grid on slide 12 is generic enough to fit any dataset.

name: Aradhya Bapna
what_worked: Crowding-then-concentration-then-B2B-filter arc is editorially tight and purposeful.
fix_next: Disclose sample sizes for the B2B/B2C AI split and reconcile the 5x claim with the reference ~2.3x median ratio.
verdict: Tight narrative, thin and unverified evidence.
factual_error_detail: Slide 2: AI share of revenue stated as 13.4%; actual is $2,356,676/$15,596,345 = 15.1% of total revenue (or ~32% of categorized revenue). The 19.7% startup share uses 197/1000 but 274 rows lack category, so the denominator choice is undisclosed and misleading. Slide 4: B2B AI median $1,357 and B2C AI median $278 are unverifiable against reference data; the overall B2B/B2C median multiple is ~2.3x, not 5x, making the '5x' headline claim suspect. Slide 3: 48% top-10 share rounds acceptably from 49.6%, but 66% AI top-10 concentration is unverifiable.

evidence.insight: The core insight—that AI is crowded but B2B AI specifically monetizes better—is a genuine analytical step beyond chart description. However, only three data points support the entire thesis, and the deck never explores alternative explanations (survivorship, category overlap, sample sizes within AI B2B/B2C splits).
evidence.narrative: Clean thesis-evidence-recommendation arc across 5 slides. Each evidence slide builds toward the final recommendation. The sequence is purposeful and the landing is clear. Loses points for being so brief that it feels more like an assertion than a demonstrated argument.
evidence.framing: Audience (investors) and question (where to allocate capital in AI) are clear. However, no mention of missingness (274 rows lack category, 288 lack audience_type), no sample sizes for the B2B/B2C AI split, no limitations, and no definition of what counts as 'AI' vs other categories. A cold reader cannot assess how robust the claims are.
evidence.accuracy: Slide 2 revenue share 13.4% is off from the correct ~15.1%. The denominator for startup share (197/1000 vs 197/726) is not disclosed. Slide 4's 5x B2B/B2C AI median claim cannot be verified and conflicts with the overall dataset B2B/B2C median ratio of ~2.3x. Slide 3's 48% is close to 49.6% (acceptable rounding) but 66% AI concentration is unverifiable. No n-values reported anywhere.
evidence.visual: Consistent dark theme with gold accent, clean typography, strong hierarchy. Bar chart on slide 2 is simple and effective. Big-number cards on slides 3-4 are legible. However, the visual palette is repetitive across slides and the deck relies entirely on big numbers rather than actual charts—no distributions, no scatterplots, no comparisons that would let the reader interrogate the data.
evidence.ai_slop: No obvious generic filler or consulting buzzwords. The prose is tight and purposeful. The visual template is consistent but not offensively generic. Minimal slop detected.

name: Arnav Singh Negi
title: Startup Delusion
what_worked: Original 'Delusion Score' metric with named case studies in a 2×2 quadrant is memorable and decision-useful.
fix_next: Disclose the 262-row subset criteria, missing-data rates, and flag n=6 and n=10 category samples as fragile.
verdict: Clever original angle, absent scope and limitations disclosure.
factual_error_detail: Slide 2: correlation of -0.14 is for a derived variable pair (asking multiple vs growth) on a 262-row subset, not verifiable against frozen data and presented without caveat. Slide 3: category rankings built on n=6 and n=10 subsets presented as definitive leaderboard positions without uncertainty acknowledgment, which borders on misleading even if technically not 'wrong.'

evidence.insight: The Delusion Score (Ask Percentile − Growth Percentile) is a genuinely original derived metric. The 2×2 quadrant with named exemplars (Rolely, DodgePrint, imposter·ai, Linkeddit) adds real texture. The 'all-in-one' vs 'AI' pitch keyword finding (slide 4, n=11 vs n=82) is a surprising non-obvious nugget, though the all-in-one n=11 is fragile.
evidence.narrative: Strong provocative thesis on slide 1, clean methodology on slide 2, category evidence on slide 3, case-study contrast on slide 4, three actionable takeaways on slide 5. The arc from provocation → method → evidence → examples → action is coherent and purposeful.
evidence.framing: TrustMRR is never explained to a cold reader beyond 'marketplace.' The 262 for-sale subset is never contextualized against the 1,000-row dataset. No mention of 274 missing categories, 216 zero-revenue rows, or 241 missing countries. No limitations slide. Target audience (buyer? seller? analyst?) is implied but never stated. A cold reader cannot assess how representative the findings are.
evidence.accuracy: The entire analysis operates on a self-selected 262-row subset with derived metrics that cannot be cross-checked against frozen reference data. The -0.14 correlation is for a different variable pair than the frozen r=0.025. Category sample sizes (n=6 E-comm, n=10 Education) are tiny yet presented as definitive rankings without confidence intervals or caveats. The 326.8× multiple and $81 revenue for Rolely are specific and plausible but unverifiable. No causal overclaims detected, which is good.
evidence.visual: Clean dark/light contrast on slides 1 and 5. Effective red/blue dichotomy for deluded/honest on slides 2-4. Slide 3's diverging horizontal bar chart is well-labeled and appropriately colored. Slide 4's side-by-side comparison cards are effective. Slide 5 is text-heavy but readable. No chart junk. Consistent typography throughout. Only one true data visualization (slide 3) for a 5-slide deck.
evidence.ai_slop: 'Zero mercy' tagline and 'Certified Genius'/'Just Vibing' labels are slightly performative but serve the narrative voice rather than being generic filler. No decorative/fabricated charts. No inflated boilerplate language. Minimal slop overall.

change_reason: Lowered framing from 6.0 to 5.5: the deck never explains TrustMRR, never states the audience, and completely omits data-quality disclosures (missing categories, zero-revenue rows, subset selection). These are material omissions for a cold reader. Other scores confirmed as appropriate after independent review.

first_pass.what_worked: Original 'Delusion Score' construct creates a genuinely novel, decision-useful lens on the marketplace data.
first_pass.fix_next: The analysis uses only 262 for-sale listings but never reconciles with the full 1,000-row dataset's revenue/category benchmarks, risking denominator confusion.
first_pass.verdict: Creative angle with strong narrative, but narrow scope and unverifiable claims limit rigor.

Slide 3: Category leaderboard uses very small n (e.g., Education n=10, E-comm n=6) without adequate caveat about instability; the deck implies these are robust rankings. Slide 4: 'AI in the pitch doesn't raise the price' claim (median 1.8× vs 2.4×) is plausible but unverifiable from frozen data and presented with unearned certainty given n=82 and n=180 on a text-mining exercise.

evidence.insight: The 'Delusion Score = Ask Percentile − Growth Percentile' is a genuinely original derived metric (slide 2). The 2×2 quadrant framework with named examples adds texture. The 'all-in-one' vs 'AI' pitch keyword finding (slide 4) is a surprising, non-obvious nugget.
evidence.narrative: Strong thesis on slide 1 ('Who's charging tomorrow's price for yesterday's growth?'), methodology on slide 2, category ranking on slide 3, case studies on slide 4, takeaways on slide 5. Clean arc from provocation → method → evidence → examples → action.
evidence.framing: The deck never explains what TrustMRR is to a cold reader beyond 'marketplace.' It doesn't mention the 274 missing categories, 216 zero-revenue rows, or how the 262 for-sale subset was identified. No limitations slide. Audience (buyer? seller? investor?) is implied but never stated.
evidence.accuracy: The deck operates on a self-selected 262-row subset with derived metrics (asking multiples, growth percentiles) that cannot be verified against the frozen dataset. Category sample sizes are tiny (n=6, n=10) yet presented as definitive rankings. The correlation of -0.14 is for a different variable pair than the frozen dataset's known r=0.025. The 326.8× multiple and $81 revenue for Rolely are specific enough to be plausible but unverifiable.
evidence.visual: Clean dark/light contrast, effective use of red/blue for deluded/honest dichotomy (slides 2-4). The horizontal bar chart on slide 3 is well-labeled with diverging color. Slide 4's side-by-side comparison cards are effective. Slide 5 is text-heavy but readable. No chart junk. Consistent typography.
evidence.ai_slop: Minimal slop. The tagline 'zero mercy' and 'Certified Genius'/'Just Vibing' labels are slightly performative but serve the narrative. No generic filler or decorative graphics.

fix_next: Category shares are fabricated (AI is 27% not 35%, SaaS 9% not 28%)—redo with actual counts and disclose 274 missing rows.
verdict: Consulting template filled with wrong category percentages.
factual_error_detail: Slide 6: AI shown as 35% and SaaS 28%—actual shares among categorized rows are AI ~27% (197/726) and SaaS ~9% (66/726); Mobile Apps 15% vs actual ~7%; Productivity 12% vs actual ~7%; percentages sum to 100% ignoring 274 missing rows and 7+ other categories. Slide 3: claims 'high correlation between MRR stability and annual growth' with no evidence or data support. Slide 6: labels 5 categories as exhaustive when dataset has 12+. Slide 3: labels chart as ARR ($M) but dataset provides 30-day revenue, not verified ARR. Slide 3: 1Lookup $3.12M ARR—dataset total 30-day revenue is $15.6M so a single company at $3.12M ARR (~$260K/month) would be ~1.7% of total, plausible but presented without sourcing the ARR conversion.

evidence.insight: Deck cherry-picks ~6 companies without exploring distributions, medians, missingness, provider patterns, or any dataset-wide patterns. No insight goes beyond listing individual company stats.
evidence.narrative: Has a logical sequence (framework → financials → growth → unit economics → screening → allocation → execution) but it reads as a generic PE pitch template filled with a handful of names rather than a data story.
evidence.framing: Slide 1 states scope and market context but never defines the dataset's limitations (274 missing categories, 216 zero-revenue companies, 241 missing countries). No audience definition beyond implied investor. TrustMRR described as 'acquisition marketplace' which mischaracterizes the dataset.
evidence.accuracy: Slide 6 category percentages are materially wrong and appear fabricated. Slide 3 claims about MRR-growth correlation are unsupported. The deck treats 30-day revenue as ARR without noting the conversion assumption. No mention of 216 zero-revenue rows or missingness rates.
evidence.visual: Consistent warm-toned template with clean typography and readable charts. However, visual sameness across slides 4-5 (identical card layouts) and pie charts used where bar charts would be more honest. No annotations or source labels on any chart.
evidence.ai_slop: Heavy consulting jargon throughout ('Pareto concentration in the top percentile,' 'high-yield long-term acquisitions,' 'downside valuation risk'). Slide 2 evaluation framework is generic filler that could apply to any dataset. Slide 10 execution steps are boilerplate PE due-diligence steps unrelated to data analysis.

name: Saksheth Akshay Rao

fix_next: Verify total revenue ($13.5M should be $15.6M), zero-revenue count (109 should be 216), and Analytics median ($1,294 vs $419).
verdict: Engaging storytelling, but half the key numbers are wrong.
factual_error_detail: Slide 1: '$13.5M combined MRR' — actual total is $15.6M, off by ~$2M. Slide 2: top-10 share stated as 48% vs reference 49.6%, minor but directionally rounded down. Slide 2: mean $13,472 implies total ~$13.5M, consistent with wrong total. Slide 3: 10.9% zero-revenue (109 cos.) vs reference 216 zero-revenue companies (21.6%) — roughly half the true figure. Slide 4: B2B/B2C median ratio claimed 5.7x ($1,036/$181); reference on-sale medians give 2.35x — even if these are full-dataset medians the magnitude is suspect and unverifiable without disclosure. Slide 6: AI median $446 vs reference $503; Content Creation median $1,254 vs reference $1,237.50 (close); Analytics median $1,294 vs reference $419 (off by ~3x); Education median $2,142 vs reference $2,435; Marketing median $1,586 vs reference $2,369.50 (off significantly). Slide 6: multiple category medians materially diverge. Slides 5-6: no disclosure of 241 missing countries or 274 missing categories affecting denominators.

evidence.insight: Slide 6 volume-vs-economics framing for AI is genuinely useful; slide 5 India Supergrow outlier analysis demonstrates analytical depth; slide 7 correlation hierarchy (subscribers vs followers) is decision-relevant.
evidence.narrative: Clear arc: concentration → audience economics → geography → category → correlations → synthesis. Slide 8 ties four takeaways back to earlier slides. Each slide has a thesis-driven title.
evidence.framing: Slide 1 states scope and data source. However, 241 missing countries (24%), 274 missing categories (27%), and 288 missing audience_type (29%) are never disclosed — this materially affects geographic, category, and B2B/B2C claims. Target audience implied but not stated.
evidence.accuracy: Total revenue off by ~$2M. Zero-revenue count understated by roughly half. Analytics median off by ~3x. Marketing median off by ~$800. B2B/B2C multiplier appears inflated vs reference. Multiple category medians diverge materially. These are not rounding issues.
evidence.visual: Consistent dark/gold palette with clear hierarchy. Appropriate chart types (horizontal bars for rankings, vertical for growth split). Labels include sample sizes. Slide 8 slightly dense but readable. No decorative or fabricated charts.
evidence.ai_slop: None detected — all slides reference specific companies, precise figures, and dataset-specific findings with no generic filler.

change_reason: Lowered accuracy from 5.0 to 4.5: confirmed 7 factual errors including total revenue off by $2M, zero-revenue count roughly halved, Analytics median off by 3x, Marketing median materially wrong, and B2B/B2C multiplier likely inflated. Lowered framing from 6.5 to 6.0 for complete omission of substantial missingness across three key fields used in analysis. Other scores unchanged as preliminary assessment was well-calibrated.

fix_next: Rebuild on the actual 1,000-row dataset—the entire deck runs on a hallucinated 8,782-row file.
verdict: Polished consulting narrative on entirely fabricated numbers.
factual_error_detail: Slide 1-2: 8,782 companies claimed vs actual 1,000 rows. Slide 1: $33.9M total revenue vs actual $15.6M. Slide 1: 117 countries vs actual far fewer (241 missing). Slide 4: 51% at $0 (implies ~4,481) vs actual 216 zero-revenue rows (21.6%). Slide 7: 560 anonymized companies vs actual 129. Slide 7: anonymized share 50% of revenue vs actual 26.5%. Slide 14: AI 751 companies vs actual 197; Productivity 237 vs not in reference top categories; SaaS 295 vs actual 66. Slide 13: Productivity shown as #1 category at $3.05M; actual top is AI at $2.36M. Slide 14: Marketing 168 companies vs actual 42. Slide 6: top-10% share 97% vs reference top-10 share 49.6%. Slide 15: US 1,577 companies — actual US count far smaller. Slide 12: top company $7.14M — not verifiable against reference total of $15.6M for entire dataset. Slide 2: 31 categories claimed vs reference shows ~11 named categories. Slide 17: 59% Stripe — reference shows 636/1000=63.6%.

evidence.insight: Billing-provider maturity as a screening proxy (slide 24), anonymized-cohort governance gap (slide 7), follower-revenue disconnect as upsell list (slide 21) are decision-useful angles that go beyond surface description, though all rest on wrong denominators.
evidence.narrative: Clear three-act structure: diagnose concentration → expose blind spots → recommend triage. Consistent section numbering, purposeful sequencing from health through SWOT to next steps, and a memorable closing line on slide 29.
evidence.framing: Slide 2 explicitly addresses methodology and data confidence tiers, which is good practice. However, the entire framing is built on the false claim of 8,782 rows when the dataset has 1,000. The 'board-level consulting review' persona is adopted without any grounding in the actual assignment. A cold reader would be misled about the dataset's scale.
evidence.accuracy: Virtually every quantitative claim is wrong by large multiples. Row count inflated 8.8x, total revenue inflated ~2.2x, zero-revenue count inflated ~20x, anonymous count inflated ~4.3x, category company counts off 3-10x, category revenue rankings reshuffled. The 97% top-decile concentration claim contradicts the reference 49.6% top-10 share. Internal consistency of the fabricated numbers does not redeem external inaccuracy.
evidence.visual: Professional, consistent dark-navy template with good hierarchy. Pareto curve (slide 6), bubble chart (slide 9), correlation heatmap (slide 22), and bar charts (slide 15) are well-chosen and labeled. Treemap (slide 13) partially illegible for small categories. Risk matrix (slide 20) has overlapping text. Overall restrained and readable.
evidence.ai_slop: Heavy consulting-template language throughout ('board-level assessment,' 'capital-allocation opportunity,' 'option book,' 'de-risk the core'). The fabrication of an internally consistent but externally wrong 8,782-row dataset with precise-looking statistics is characteristic of LLM confabulation. SWOT slide is formulaic.

change_reason: Lowered accuracy from 2.5 to 2.0: upon closer review, at least 14 distinct factual errors identified, with the foundational dataset size wrong by 8.8x — this is not rounding error but wholesale fabrication. Lowered framing from 5 to 4.5: the methodology slide's claim of a larger dataset actively misleads rather than contextualizes. Removed bonus point: while the consulting framing is polished, the work cannot merit bonus when its entire quantitative foundation is hallucinated.

name: Nikhil Rudra H P
title: Emerging startups in Europe
what_worked: Structured elimination of alternatives and honest labeling of subjective scoring show self-awareness.
fix_next: Derive claims from the assigned dataset—9 of 10 slides rely on external market reports, making this a pitch deck not a data story.
verdict: Consulting pitch that ignores the assigned data.
factual_error_detail: Slide 5: Claims '289 are Europe-based' and '74 of 289 European listings' in AI — the dataset has 241 missing country values and no 'Europe' filter yields 289; the dataset contains no geographic region field that cleanly produces this number, and Health & Fitness has only 34 companies total (not a large vertical). Slide 5: States AI is largest category among European listings at 74 — cannot be verified and likely fabricated given missing-country rate. Slide 1/throughout: Presents the deck as analyzing the provided 1,000-row dataset for European startup trends, but the dataset is a global revenue-tracking list with no VC funding data, no European-specific funding figures, and no industry growth rates — virtually all quantitative claims ($63.8B, $17.5B AI VC, +15% digital health, 65% AI-powered share, etc.) come from external sources with no verifiable connection to the assigned data.

evidence.insight: The recommendation (Applied Health AI) is a reasonable consulting conclusion but is not derived from the assigned dataset. The scoring framework on slide 6 is entirely subjective author judgment. No novel analytical finding emerges from the 1,000-row dataset.
evidence.narrative: Clear 10-section arc from ecosystem overview → vertical screening → gap analysis → recommendation → business model → roadmap. Logical flow, but repetitive — the same five bullet points (fastest vertical, €14B+, demographic tailwind, regulatory moat, evidence bar) appear on slides 1, 4, 6, 8, and 10.
evidence.framing: Slide 1 states the objective clearly, but the framing implies the analysis is driven by the provided dataset when it is overwhelmingly driven by external market reports. The dataset is mentioned only on slide 5 as a 'bottom-up cross-check' with unverifiable numbers. No limitations about the mismatch between dataset scope and analysis scope are disclosed.
evidence.accuracy: Nearly all quantitative claims ($63.8B European VC, $17.5B AI, +15% digital health, 65% AI-powered, €20B InvestAI) are from external sources and cannot be verified against the assigned dataset. The one dataset-derived claim (289 European companies, 74 in AI) is suspect given 241 missing country values and no clear methodology shown. The dataset contains no VC funding amounts, no European funding totals, and no growth rates — it tracks 30-day MRR for small startups.
evidence.visual: Consistent dark-theme design with good typography hierarchy, readable tables, and appropriate chart types (bar, line). The 2x3 stat grid on slide 4 is clean. Some text density issues on slides 5 and 8. No chart dishonesty in the charts shown, though the charts represent external data.
evidence.ai_slop: Heavy consulting-framework stacking (SWOT + Porter's + PESTLE + Blue Ocean matrix + Business Model Canvas + TAM/SAM/SOM) without depth in any. The 'Confidential Draft' footer is performative. The scoring matrix on slide 6 uses round subjective numbers presented as analytical output. Repetition of the same five talking points across multiple slides.

what_worked: Side-by-side company comparison format with custom KPIs is a genuinely useful decision-making layout.
fix_next: Two slides profiling four cherry-picked companies is not a data story—add dataset-level analysis, framing, and a thesis.
verdict: Polished company cards with no dataset story or analytical depth.
factual_error_detail: Slide 1: Cometly 'Recurring rev. share 107%' is mathematically impossible as a share and unexplained. Slide 2: Pattrn labeled '0%' growth but went from $0 to $2.7K—0% is misleading (undefined, not zero). Six-month revenue trajectories are presented as modeled but no model or source is disclosed, making all trend figures unverifiable against the dataset.

evidence.insight: Slides show four individual company profiles with custom metrics (ARPU, AUD, VEL, MIX) which add some analytical texture, but no broader patterns, distributions, or dataset-level findings are offered. The 'picks' are unexplained selections with no criteria disclosed.
evidence.narrative: There is no thesis, no introduction, no conclusion, no connection to the broader dataset. Two slides of paired comparisons do not form a coherent story arc—just a listicle of company snapshots.
evidence.framing: No audience is stated, no research question is posed, no scope or dataset description is given. A cold reader has no idea what dataset this draws from, what 'safety pick' or 'growth pick' means operationally, or why these four companies were chosen from 1,000.
evidence.accuracy: 107% recurring revenue share is nonsensical without explanation. 0% growth for Pattrn ($0→$2.7K) is misleading. The six-month revenue bars are described as 'modeled from each company's reported totals' but no methodology is given, making all figures unverifiable. Metrics like 'Rev. velocity (lifetime)' are undefined.
evidence.visual: Consistent card-based layout with clear hierarchy, color-coded KPI badges, and readable bar charts. The template is well-executed and visually clean. However, the two slides are nearly identical in structure, and the decorative blob adds nothing.
evidence.ai_slop: Template repetition across both slides is notable—identical layout with only color swaps (purple vs. gold). The format feels like a polished AI-generated card template applied twice without variation.

name: Athrv Thakuria
what_worked: Restrained visual design with consistent hierarchy; stealth/anonymous analysis adds a less-obvious angle.
fix_next: Add a thesis and limitations slide—this reads as a dashboard summary, not a data story.
verdict: Accurate dashboard tour lacking a thesis or deeper insight.
factual_error_detail: Slide 7: 131 stealth startups vs reference 129 anonymous companies (minor). Slide 7: $4.2M / 27% stealth revenue vs reference 26.525% (~$4.13M) — close but slightly inflated. Slide 3: Top-10 share stated as 50% vs reference 49.6% — acceptable rounding. Slide 5: '26% of startups' for US — 258/1000 is 25.8%, but 258 out of 759 with known country is 34%; denominator choice unclear and not disclosed.

evidence.insight: Findings are real but surface-level: concentration, AI leads, B2B > B2C, US dominance. No surprising cross-cuts, no median-vs-mean discussion for categories, no provider analysis, no founded-year exploration. The stealth observation (slide 7) is the most original point but still descriptive.
evidence.narrative: Slides proceed topic-by-topic (snapshot → concentration → categories → geography → marketplace → growth → takeaways) without a unifying thesis or argument. The takeaway slide repeats prior slides verbatim. No synthesis or 'so what' beyond listing facts.
evidence.framing: No stated audience, question, or scope. No mention of missingness (274 missing category, 241 missing country, 288 missing audience_type). The 'market tags' on slide 4 appear to be a different field than 'category' but this is never explained. No limitations slide.
evidence.accuracy: Core numbers are largely correct: $15.6M total, 1000 startups, AI $2.4M/197, Marketing $1.3M/42, E-comm $1.1M/19, top-10 ~50%. B2B/B2C medians plausible. Stealth count 131 vs 129 is a minor discrepancy. US denominator issue (26% of all 1000 vs % of known-country) is not disclosed. Revenue tier table sums to 1000 which is fine.
evidence.visual: Consistent card-based layout, good use of teal accent color, legible typography, proper footer with source. Only one actual chart (bar chart on slide 6). Heavy reliance on big-number cards becomes repetitive across 6 slides. No scatter plots, distributions, or richer visualizations. The bar chart on slide 6 has a minor label overlap issue.
evidence.ai_slop: Template is uniform but not egregiously generic. No decorative meaningless graphics. Some consulting-style phrasing ('volume play', 'commands higher ARPU') but restrained. The repetitive card layout across nearly every slide borders on template sameness.

name: Ayushi Uniyal
what_worked: Three-decision structure with synthesis slide and explicit causal discipline on slide 8 is genuinely rare.
fix_next: Disclose missingness (274 categories, 216 zero-revenue, 288 audience_type) and show sample sizes next to every median.
verdict: Well-structured decision deck weakened by missing-data silence.
factual_error_detail: Slide 2: Spearman correlations stated without verifiable basis; values plausible but unconfirmable. Slide 7 median values are in reasonable range but cannot be exactly verified. Slide 5 acquisition targets are dataset-specific and unverifiable but not necessarily wrong. No hard factual contradiction found except: the deck never acknowledges ~27% missing category data or 216 zero-revenue rows, which materially affects median calculations presented as authoritative—this is an accuracy-by-omission issue rather than a discrete factual error. Counting conservatively as 1 for the omission that distorts interpretation.

evidence.insight: Slide 2 correlation hierarchy (followers 0.17 vs subscriptions-MRR 0.90) is a useful finding; slide 8 causality check is rare and valuable. But the 'build' recommendation (revenue-health copilot) is a startup pitch extrapolated well beyond dataset evidence—more imagination than insight.
evidence.narrative: Clear build/buy/pay three-act arc with slide 9 synthesis and slide 10 action plan. 'One portfolio logic' line ties decisions together. Sequence is purposeful. Landing is concrete with measurable proof points.
evidence.framing: Slide 1 sets up three questions clearly; audience (indie SaaS founder) is identifiable. However, dataset limitations are never disclosed: 274 missing categories, 216 zero-revenue rows, 288 missing audience_type, 241 missing country. This is a significant framing gap that a cold reader needs. Downgraded from preliminary 7.0.
evidence.accuracy: Provider counts (636, 189) match reference. Median revenue figures on slide 7 are plausible but unverifiable. Acquisition data on slide 5 is specific to named companies and unverifiable. Zero-revenue rows and missingness are never acknowledged despite materially affecting medians. No outright false number contradicts the reference, but omission of data quality context is an accuracy concern.
evidence.visual: Clean typography, consistent color coding, good hierarchy. Slide 2 and 7 bar charts are clear. Slide 2 has visible text truncation ('Implicatio/n', 'conversio/n'). Slide 3 colored blocks are decorative not informative. Slide 6 progress bars lack scale. Overall competent but not polished.
evidence.ai_slop: Slide 3 'revenue-health copilot' and slide 5 'conversational revenue OS' feel like startup pitch template language. Slide 4 business model canvas is more pitch than data story. Generally restrained but consulting-speak appears in places.

change_reason: Reduced framing from 7.0 to 6.0 because complete silence on missingness and zero-revenue rows is a material gap for a data story. Reduced bonus from 2 to 1: the causality check on slide 8 is genuinely good but the startup-pitch slides (3-4) dilute the data-story merit. Other scores unchanged.

first_pass.what_worked: Strong three-decision thesis with explicit causal discipline on slide 8 and honest diligence gates on slide 6.
first_pass.fix_next: Verify median revenue figures against the frozen dataset—Stripe median, Paddle median, and others appear fabricated or miscalculated, undermining the payments argument.
first_pass.verdict: Coherent strategic narrative undermined by unverifiable median figures and thin dataset engagement.
first_pass.factual_error_detail: Slide 7: Stripe median shown as $735 vs no direct reference but plausible; RevenueCat median $309 vs reference not directly given for median revenue but total/count suggests different; Paddle median $138 vs reference $96,742/16≈$6,046 total but median not directly given; Lemon Squeezy $38 vs reference $140,414/25 total—medians are plausible but Dodo shown as $9 while Polar $0 are roughly consistent. Slide 7: Dodo median $9 is plausible given $38,693/50. However the claim 'strongest median revenue among general-purpose web providers' conflates selection bias with provider quality without noting sample composition differences. Slide 2: Spearman correlations (0.89, 0.90, 0.60, 0.17) are stated without verification possible against reference—not counted as errors but unverifiable. Slide 5: SetSmart acquisition figures ($499k ask, $15.7k MRR, +29% rev growth, +100% MRR growth, 0.8× multiple) are presented as dataset facts but cannot be verified against reference and may be cherry-picked or fabricated. Slide 3: Omits Dodo (50), Superwall (17), Polar (36) from provider landscape while claiming to show fragmentation. Slide 4: Claims 'crowded categories with weak median economics' for productivity/social but doesn't show the data. Material errors: (1) Provider counts on slide 3 selectively omit 3 providers while framing as comprehensive, (2) No acknowledgment of 274 missing category values or 286 missing domain values affecting build thesis, (3) No mention of 216 zero-revenue companies affecting median calculations, (4) Acquisition slide presents specific company data without sourcing or acknowledging these may not be verifiable from the frozen dataset.

evidence.insight: Slide 2 offers a useful hierarchy of correlation strengths; slide 4 proposes a specific product concept grounded in observed fragmentation; slide 6 provides a genuine diligence framework. However, the 'build' recommendation (revenue-health copilot) is more startup pitch than dataset insight—it extrapolates far beyond what the data shows.
evidence.narrative: Clear three-act structure (build/buy/pay) with synthesis on slide 9 and actionable 90-day plan on slide 10. The 'one portfolio logic' line ties the three decisions together. Sequence is purposeful and each slide advances the argument.
evidence.framing: Slide 1 sets up three questions clearly. Audience (indie SaaS founder) is implicit but identifiable. However, dataset limitations (274 missing categories, 216 zero-revenue rows, 288 missing audience_type) are never disclosed, which is a significant framing gap for a data-story.
evidence.accuracy: Provider counts on slide 3 (636, 189, 16, 25) match reference for Stripe, RevenueCat, Paddle, Lemon Squeezy. Median revenue figures on slide 7 cannot be fully verified but are in plausible ranges for some providers. The acquisition target data on slide 5 is entirely unverifiable. Missing data is never acknowledged. The correlation figures on slide 2 are stated as Spearman but unverifiable.
evidence.visual: Clean, consistent layout with good hierarchy and readable typography. Color coding is consistent across slides. Bar charts on slides 2 and 7 are clear. However, the colored blocks on slide 3 are decorative rather than informative, and the progress-bar-style indicators on slide 6 have no clear scale or meaning. Some text truncation visible on slide 2 ('Implication' and 'conversion' are cut off).
evidence.ai_slop: Slide 3 'revenue-health copilot' concept and slide 4 business model canvas feel like startup pitch template output rather than data-driven findings. The colored rounded rectangles on slide 3 are decorative. 'Conversational revenue OS' on slide 5 is inflated consulting language. Generally restrained but some consulting-speak creeps in.

name: Bhavya Jain
what_worked: Screening funnel with named targets, explicit filter criteria, and honest risk caveats is genuinely decision-useful.
fix_next: Verify category medians on slide 5—several diverge materially from reference data and Analytics ranking is wrong.
verdict: Sharp investor memo with real analytical teeth, dinged by wrong medians.
factual_error_detail: Slide 4: 197 $0-revenue listings stated; reference says 216. Slide 5: Category medians diverge substantially from reference — Education shown $2,142 vs ref $2,435; Marketing $1,586 vs ref $2,369.50; Analytics $1,294 vs ref $419; Content Creation $1,254 vs ref $1,237.50; AI $446 vs ref $503; SaaS $303 vs ref $200.50. Several are directionally wrong in ranking (Analytics shown above Marketing). Slide 6: Stripe share stated as 64% (≈636/1000 is 63.6%, acceptable rounding, but denominator ambiguity). Slide 2: '19% growing >10%' stated but slide 7 shows 12%+8%=20% — internal inconsistency.

evidence.insight: Slides 10-13 go well beyond chart description: identifying specific acquisition targets with price/fundamentals mismatches, flagging 18 overpriced declining assets, and articulating a micro-PE thesis (slide 15). The correlation analysis on slide 8 yields a concrete diligence recommendation. The 'avoid' list on slide 13 is genuinely useful negative screening.
evidence.narrative: Clear funnel structure: landscape → performance → screening → targets → risks → thesis → next steps. Each slide builds toward the investment recommendation. The executive summary (slide 2) previews all key findings. Slide 17 closes with a crisp bottom line. No orphan slides.
evidence.framing: Slide 3 explicitly defines the dataset, known gaps (traffic 18%, category 27%, country 24%, anonymized 13%), and screening logic. Audience (Investment Committee) is stated on every slide footer. Slide 14 enumerates five specific caveats including self-reported financials and single-month growth limitations. Scope is well-bounded.
evidence.accuracy: Slide 4: $0-revenue count is 197 vs reference 216 — material error affecting the funnel math (803 vs correct 784). Slide 5: Multiple category medians are wrong — Analytics at $1,294 vs ref $419 is a 3x overstatement; Education at $2,142 vs ref $2,435; Marketing at $1,586 vs ref $2,369.50. These errors affect the category ranking and the 'revenue quality' narrative. Slide 2 says 19% growing >10% but slide 7 shows 20% (12%+8%). The 48x mean/median gap and 38x median multiple claims are not directly verifiable but plausible. Correlation figures on slide 8 appear reasonable but cannot be fully verified.
evidence.visual: Consistent navy/gold/red color scheme throughout. Charts are simple and appropriate (bar charts, donut, funnel). Tables on slides 10 and 13 are clean and scannable. Big-number callouts are well-sized. Slide 7 pie chart is the weakest visual — hard to read segment sizes. No decorative graphics. Consistent footer and slide numbering. Good restraint overall.
evidence.ai_slop: none — the deck avoids generic filler, consulting buzzwords, and decorative graphics. Every slide carries dataset-specific content. The investment-memo framing is appropriate to the stated audience rather than inflated.

name: Bhavya Tuteja
what_worked: Topography metaphor is sustained coherently across slides with a chaos-to-prescription arc.
fix_next: Replace every illustrative schematic with real data charts showing actual values, axes, and sample sizes.
verdict: Consulting theater with no real data—illustrations masquerade as analysis.
factual_error_detail: Slide 1/title: frames dataset as 'SaaS Market' when it covers AI, Marketing, E-comm, Education, etc. Slide 7: table dimensions (product velocity, churn rate, pricing power) do not exist in the dataset—entirely fabricated. Slide 5: claims about Domain Rating vs X Followers as archetype drivers are asserted without any supporting correlation or data. Slide 3: quadrant scatter presented as data-derived but has no axis values, thresholds, or sample sizes—appears wholly illustrative.

evidence.insight: Core thesis (social attention → domain authority → MRR) is a plausible strategic idea but never substantiated with a single number from the dataset. No category, provider, TLD, or revenue analysis appears anywhere.
evidence.narrative: Arc is purposeful: chaos → framework → archetypes → drivers → anomalies → prescriptions → conclusion. Topography metaphor holds. But the narrative is built entirely on assertions, making it a story about a story rather than a data story.
evidence.framing: Title says 'SaaS Market' but dataset spans all categories. No mention of 1,000 rows, 216 zero-revenue entries, or 24–29% missingness across key fields. No audience specified. Scope and limitations entirely absent.
evidence.accuracy: Not a single verifiable figure from the frozen reference appears. Slide 6 cites 'Stealth Co 17, 718% growth' and slide 8 cites '12,983% MRR growth jump'—specific but unverifiable. Slide 7's four dimensions are fabricated columns not in the dataset. Zero revenue totals, medians, category counts, or provider shares shown.
evidence.visual: Illustrations are stylistically consistent and polished (NotebookLM-generated). However, every 'chart' (slides 3, 6, 8, 9) is a schematic illustration, not a data visualization—no real axes, values, or labels. This is decorative design, not evidence-led design. Downgraded from preliminary for decorative/fabricated charts.
evidence.ai_slop: Pervasive: 'operational velocity,' 'structural authority,' 'weaponise capital,' 'forensic audit of churn drivers,' 'existential timer,' 'fleeting social noise → permanent structural authority.' Slide 7 is generic SaaS consulting boilerplate. Every illustration is AI-generated decoration.

change_reason: Lowered framing by 0.5 (scope mislabeled, zero limitations) and visual by 0.5 (all charts are decorative schematics, not data visualizations—penalized per rubric for fabricated/decorative charts). Other scores confirmed as appropriate.

first_pass.what_worked: Consistent topography metaphor and the anomaly-validation framework on slides 8–9 showed genuine analytical thinking.
first_pass.fix_next: Nearly every chart is decorative illustration, not data-driven; ground claims in actual dataset numbers, categories, providers, and sample sizes.
first_pass.verdict: Polished consulting theater with almost no verifiable data behind it.
first_pass.factual_error_detail: S1: calls it 'thousands of SaaS entities' — dataset has 1,000 rows. S2: same 'thousands' claim. S3: quadrant scatter appears fabricated — no axes with real units, no thresholds defined, no evidence these clusters exist in the data. S7: 'Anatomy of Outperformance' table claims about churn, pricing power, product velocity are entirely invented — none of these variables exist in the dataset. S4/S5: causal pipeline from X Followers → Domain Rating → MRR is asserted without correlation evidence or controlling for confounders; dataset has observational associations only.

evidence.insight: The core thesis (convert social attention into domain authority) is a plausible strategic idea but is never substantiated with any actual numbers from the dataset. No category analysis, no provider analysis, no revenue distributions, no median comparisons. Slide 7's table is pure invention — churn rate, pricing power, product velocity are not in the dataset.
evidence.narrative: There is a coherent arc: chaos → framework → archetypes → drivers → anomalies → prescriptions → conclusion. The sequence is purposeful and the topography metaphor holds. However, the narrative is built on assertions rather than evidence, making it a story about a story rather than a data story.
evidence.framing: Title says 'SaaS Market' but the dataset covers all categories (AI, Marketing, E-comm, Education, etc.), not just SaaS. No mention of dataset size (1,000 rows), missingness (241–288 across fields), or the 216 zero-revenue companies. No audience is specified. Scope is undefined.
evidence.accuracy: Slide 3's quadrant chart has no real axis values, thresholds, or n-counts — it appears entirely illustrative. Slide 6 cites 'Stealth Co 17, 718% growth' which cannot be verified but is at least specific. Slide 8 cites '12,983% MRR growth jump' — plausible but unverifiable. Slide 7's four dimensions (product velocity, churn rate, pricing power) do not exist in the dataset. No actual revenue figures, category breakdowns, provider shares, or statistical measures appear anywhere in the deck.
evidence.visual: Illustrations are polished and consistent in style (NotebookLM-generated). The topography/mechanical metaphors are visually appealing. However, not a single chart shows real data with proper axes, labels, and values. The slide 3 scatter, slide 6 radar, slides 8–9 line charts are all schematic illustrations, not data visualizations. This is decorative design, not evidence-led design.
evidence.ai_slop: Heavy AI slop throughout: 'operational velocity,' 'structural authority,' 'weaponise capital,' 'forensic audit of churn drivers,' 'existential timer,' 'fleeting social noise → permanent structural authority.' Slide 7's entire comparison table is generic SaaS consulting boilerplate with no dataset grounding. Every illustration is AI-generated decoration rather than a data chart.

name: DEEPANSHU GUPTA
title: Behind the Curtains
what_worked: Crowded-vs-profitable thesis and acquisition funnel (262→224→6) show genuine analytical ambition.
fix_next: Verify category medians against source data—Education, Marketing, AI, and B2B/B2C multiplier are all materially wrong.
verdict: Compelling story with wrong category medians throughout.
factual_error_detail: Slide 3: AI median shown $446 (ref $503); Education median $2,141.50 (ref $2,435); Marketing median $1,586 (ref $2,369.50). Slide 5: B2B median multiplier claimed 5.7x ($1,036/$181) but reference shows ~2.35x median multiple; the absolute medians themselves don't match reference benchmarks. Slide 7: Analytics listed among 'highest medians' but its reference median ($419) is below AI's.

evidence.insight: Slide 6 acquisition funnel (262→224→6) is genuinely useful original analysis; slide 3 crowded≠profitable thesis is a real insight even if numbers are off; B2B premium observation is directionally correct.
evidence.narrative: Clear thesis: concentration matters, medians beat means, then category→geography→audience→acquisition pipeline. Each slide builds toward the final recommendations. Landing slide ties back with appropriate caveats.
evidence.framing: Slide 1 sets scope (1,000 startups, 65 countries, 29 categories). Audience implied as acquirer/investor but never explicitly stated. Missing-data rates (241-288 rows) never acknowledged despite affecting category and geography conclusions. Slide 7 footer adds a useful 'verify before acting' caveat.
evidence.accuracy: Three category medians are materially wrong on slide 3. B2B 5.7x multiplier on slide 5 is inflated vs reference ~2.35x. Slide 2 median $282 and mean $13,472 are plausible but unverifiable against reference (mean ≈$15,596). Education count omitted on slide 3. The 48x ratio claim on slide 2 checks out against stated numbers ($13,472/$282≈47.8).
evidence.visual: Consistent color palette (orange/dark grey), strong typographic hierarchy, effective use of proportional circles on slide 4, clean dot-array funnel on slide 6. Slide 2 median-vs-mean bubble comparison is memorable. Chart choices are appropriate throughout. Minor: slide 3 Education bar lacks count label.
evidence.ai_slop: NotebookLM watermark visible on every slide. Design is polished but not generic template-feeling. Icons on slide 7 are slightly stock-like but not egregious. No meaningless filler text detected.

name: Diksha Matia
what_worked: Exceptional narrative arc from universe to shortlist with honest risk framing and causal discipline throughout.
fix_next: Fix category counts and medians on slide 4—AI median $4.3k vs actual $503 is a massive error.
verdict: Sharp investor memo with inaccurate category figures.
factual_error_detail: Slide 4: AI median shown as $4.3k, actual is $503 (massive error). Education count ~45 vs actual 30. Marketing count ~60 vs actual 42. Dev Tools count ~40 vs actual 37. Analytics count ~35 vs actual 19. The B2B median of $8.4k on slide 4 cannot be directly verified but the reference B2B median multiple is 2.35x, not the ~3.8x gap implied.

evidence.insight: Slide 5 funnel from 1,000→3-5 is genuinely decision-useful. Slide 7 valuation trap analysis (0.0x listings = broken not bargains) shows original thinking. Slide 6 names specific companies with verify/hold flags showing intellectual honesty.
evidence.narrative: Clean arc: executive summary (S1) → distribution reality (S2) → on-sale pool (S3) → segment signals (S4) → screening funnel (S5) → shortlist (S6) → risk matrix (S7) → recommendation (S8). Each slide builds on the prior. The thesis 'buy a short list, not the market' is established on S1 and paid off on S8.
evidence.framing: Slide 1 immediately establishes audience (investor/acquirer), scope (1,000 listings as sourcing universe), and the core question. Footer assumptions/risks on every slide. Limitations called out explicitly (missing categories, subscription vs one-off mixing on S2, no margin/churn data on S7).
evidence.accuracy: Slide 2: median $3.1k and mean $133.8k are plausible but the dataset field is 30-day revenue not 12M (label says '12-MONTH REVENUE' but source says REVENUE_12M_USD—ambiguous). Slide 4 category figures are substantially wrong: AI median $4.3k vs reference $503; Education count ~45 vs 30; Marketing ~60 vs 42; Analytics ~35 vs 19. Slide 1 mean $133.8k is plausible if computed on non-zero subset but not clearly stated.
evidence.visual: Dark-mode terminal aesthetic is consistent across all 8 slides. Monospace headers, color-coded signals (green/yellow/red), clean card layouts. Slide 5 funnel visualization is effective. Slide 7 scatter plot with quadrant labels is well-annotated. No chartjunk. Restraint in decoration. Hierarchy is clear with section labels, headlines, and supporting text.
evidence.ai_slop: none — the deck avoids generic filler, uses specific numbers and company names, includes self-skeptical verify flags, and maintains a distinctive editorial voice throughout

fix_next: Use the actual assigned dataset—every revenue figure, company name, and metric appears fabricated.

name: Harnoor kaur dhanjal
title: Micro saas market intelligence
what_worked: Growth-bucket mispricing analysis and acquisition screening table show genuine analytical ambition.

verdict: Polished deck built on the wrong dataset entirely.

first_pass.fix_next: Several key numbers are materially wrong (AI total revenue, AI median, Education median, B2B/B2C median ratio); verify every figure against the frozen dataset.
first_pass.verdict: Compelling narrative and polished design undermined by multiple inaccurate figures.
first_pass.factual_error_detail: Slide 5: AI total revenue shown as $1.81M; actual is $2.36M. AI median shown as $446; actual is $503. Education median shown as $2,142; actual is $2,435. Customer Support median $5,163 not verifiable from reference categories. B2B median $1,036 and B2C median $181 yield 5.7× ratio; reference shows ~2.35×/2.30× median multiples (not the same metric but the claimed medians appear fabricated). Slide 7 title 'SEO authority drives revenue' implies causation from observational cross-sectional data.

evidence.insight: Slides 4-6 build the volume≠quality argument across category counts, median MRR, and revenue-per-visitor—a genuinely useful layered insight. The traffic conversion analysis (slide 6) adds an original angle. However, the 'two predictors' claim on slide 9 overstates what cross-sectional observational data can support.
evidence.narrative: Clear numbered progression (01-08) with a single thesis ('popularity ≠ quality') introduced on slide 4 and landed on slide 9. Each section builds on the prior. The bottom-line statement is crisp. Slight weakness: slides 2-3 are setup-heavy before the story begins.
evidence.framing: Slide 2 explains the data source, verification model, and limitations. Slide 3 shows missingness rates with a ~30% caveat. Slide 6 flags ~18% visitor coverage. Slide 9 explicitly calls out self-selection bias. Audience is implicitly indie founders/acquirers. Strong overall framing.
evidence.accuracy: Multiple figures deviate materially from the frozen reference: AI total ($1.81M vs $2.36M), AI median ($446 vs $503), Education median ($2,142 vs $2,435). The B2B/B2C medians ($1,036/$181) don't match reference multiples (2.35×/2.30×). 'Customer Support' as highest median category is unverifiable. Anonymous count 130 is close to 129 (acceptable rounding). Category missing 27.4% matches 274/1000. The 'drives' language on slide 7 is causal overreach.
evidence.visual: Consistent dark theme with restrained green/orange/yellow palette. Good hierarchy: large headline numbers, supporting annotations, source lines on every slide. Bar charts are clean and labeled. Donut chart on slide 8 is appropriate. The left bar chart on slide 6 lacks y-axis labels. Overall high craft with purposeful color coding (orange for warnings/AI underperformance).
evidence.ai_slop: none — the deck avoids generic filler, each slide has specific data points and interpretive annotations rather than boilerplate
